# Apply to VNS
## Charter School Admission
### Ready to Apply?
We’re excited to welcome new students to our AASD charter schools! The application window for the **2027–2028 school year**will open December 1, 2026.
To be included in the lottery, please submit your application by **February 19, 2027**. Applications received after that date will be added to the waiting list (if no seats are available) in the order they come in.
All families will be notified by**March 1, 2027**,and will then have the opportunity to accept or decline their seat.
The application portal will stay open through **September 1, 2027**. After that, you can contact the charter school directly to ask about current openings.

# Apply to VNS
## Charter School Admission
### Looking to join us for the 2026–2027 school year?
Enrollment availability varies by charter school—some schools have openings, while others have waitlists. We encourage you to contact your preferred charter school to learn about current availability.

# Apply to VNS
## Deciding if VNS is Right for Your Student
Valley New School is open to all students entering grades 6-12, provided they complete all parts of the application and fully understand the expectations of this educational model.
Our project-based environment is very different from the traditional school setting; taking time to understand these differences will help your family make an educated decision about whether to apply to VNS.

# Apply to VNS
## Deciding if VNS is Right for Your Student
#### 1. Get an overview
Review our website and watch videosto get a basic understanding of our school, project-based learning, and the benefits of a VNS education.

# Apply to VNS
## Deciding if VNS is Right for Your Student
#### 2. Attend a Public Informational Meeting
Advisors, with the help of parents and students, will explain the academic process and school culture as well as answer questions. Attendance at one of these meetings is required to activate a student’s application in the VNS lottery.
**For interest in the 2027-2028 school year, we offer the following public information meetings from 7:00 - 8:00 p.m.:**
*   Monday, December 7, 2026  
*   Thursday, January 21, 2027  
*   Wednesday, February 3, 2027  
*   Wednesday, February 10, 2027

# Apply to VNS
## Deciding if VNS is Right for Your Student
#### 3. Schedule a tour of VNS
See our school in action and learn more about what project-based learning offers from our Student Ambassadors and an Advisor. Please call to make an appointment: (920) 852-5605.

# Apply to VNS
## Deciding if VNS is Right for Your Student
#### 4. Schedule a ½-day shadow experience
Experience what it is really like to be a Valley New School student.Individual shadow days are always welcome, but we offer two specific shadow days with specially planned activities.Please call to register: (920) 852-5605.
*   Tuesday, January 19, 2027 and Monday, February 1, 2027

# Apply to VNS
## Deciding if VNS is Right for Your Student
#### 5. Discuss: Will VNS be the optimal learning environment for your child?
What characteristics/work habits/interests does your child possess that would make him/her successful at VNS? What aspects of VNS might be challenging/frustrating? It is imperative that both students and parents realize that VNS provides a rigorous educational program within a flexible structure. Success within this model relies strongly on the student’s motivation and the degree of parental involvement.

# Apply to VNS
## Deciding if VNS is Right for Your Student
#### 6.Submit the online application by the third Friday in February
Online application for all Appleton Area Charter Schools begins December 1. Openings and waiting list spots will be filled through a lottery drawing during the first week of March. Families are notified of status by the second Friday in March.
Siblings of current students and children of VNS staff/Governance Board members are afforded enrollment preference. Applications submitted after the deadline are added to the waiting list in the order that they are received.

# Apply to VNS
## Deciding if VNS is Right for Your Student
#### 7.For families who resideoutsideof Appleton only: Submit the Open Enrollment Application.

#### Open Enrollment
If a studentresidesin the Appleton Area School District and completes the charter school application process, they**do not**need to complete the district’s School of Choice Open Enrollment application.
TheOpen Enrollment(OE) process is separate from the charter school student application process.
Students living outside the Appleton Area School District**must apply**for Open Enrollment through the Department of Public Instruction (DPI) between early February and the end of April,in addition to completing the charter school application process.Click here for more information on open enrollment to the Appleton Area School District.
_Many students receive notification of approval to enroll in a charter school. However, different factors are taken into account that may prohibit acceptance into the AASD. Your child’s enrollment, therefore, will not be official until accepted by the District for open enrollment. Notification of the District’s decision is sent to families in the first week of June. If you accept the charter school spot now, we will hold your student's spot until that time._

The **Northern Valley Regional High School District** is a comprehensive regional publichighschool district composed of two publichigh schools serving students in ninth through twelfth grades from Closter, Demarest, Harrington Park, Haworth, Northvale, Norwood and Old Tappan, suburban communities in Bergen County, in the U.S. state of New Jersey.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Valley_Regional_High_School_District#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Valley_Regional_High_School_District#cite_note-4) Students from Rockleigh attend the district as part of a sending/receiving relationship.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Valley_Regional_High_School_District#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Valley_Regional_High_School_District#cite_note-6)
As of the 2023–24 school year, the district, comprised of three schools, had an enrollment of 2,159 students and 236.1 classroom teachers (on an FTE basis), for a student–teacher ratio of 9.1:1.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Valley_Regional_High_School_District#cite_note-NCES-1)
The communities in the district, made up of upper-middle income families, consistently support the school budget, which provides for varied, in-depth college preparatory and career-oriented curricula. Courses range from the remedial to Advanced Placement.
The district participates in special education programs offered by Region III, one of seven such regional programs in Bergen County. Region III coordinates and develops special education programs for the 1,000 students with learning disabilities in the region, which includes the Northern Valley District, as well as those for the Alpine, Closter, Demarest, Harrington Park, Haworth, Northvale, Norwood and Old Tappan districts.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Valley_Regional_High_School_District#cite_note-7)

The district's first high school facility opened in Demarest in September 1955, before which students from the constituent municipalities attended Closter High School, Dumont High School or Tenafly High School.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Valley_Regional_High_School_District#cite_note-8)
After voters rejected a June 1959 referendum that would have raised $3.25 million for construction of the district's second high school in Old Tappan, voters narrowly approved a trimmed-down version of the plan in January 1960 that reduced the cost to $2.9 million (equivalent to $31.6 million in 2025). [[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Valley_Regional_High_School_District#cite_note-9)
The Old Tappan school was opened with 740 students between the 9th and 11th grades in March 1962 to address overcrowding in the district's original school at Demarest that had been holding split sessions before the new school opened.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Valley_Regional_High_School_District#cite_note-10) At its establishment, Northern Valley Old Tappan served students from Harrington Park, Northvale, Norwood and Old Tappan, as well as those from the northern portion of Closter.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Valley_Regional_High_School_District#cite_note-11)
The district had been classified by the New Jersey Department of Education as being in District Factor Group "I", the second-highest of eight groupings. District Factor Groups organize districts statewide to allow comparison by common socioeconomic characteristics of the local districts. From lowest socioeconomic status to highest, the categories are A, B, CD, DE, FG, GH, I and J.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Valley_Regional_High_School_District#cite_note-12)

## Awards, recognition and rankings
Core members of the district's administration are:[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Valley_Regional_High_School_District#cite_note-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Valley_Regional_High_School_District#cite_note-28)
*   James Santana, superintendent[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Valley_Regional_High_School_District#cite_note-29)  
*   Marc Capizzi, business administrator and board secretary
The district's board of education, comprised of nine members, sets policy and oversees the fiscal and educational operation of the district through its administration. As a Type II school district, the board's trustees are elected directly by voters to serve three-year terms of office on a staggered basis, with three seats up for election each year held (since 2012) as part of the November general election. The board appoints a superintendent to oversee the district's day-to-day operations and a business administrator to supervise the business functions of the district.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Valley_Regional_High_School_District#cite_note-30) Seats on the board of education are allocated based on the population of the constituent municipalities, with two seats each allocated to Closter and Old Tappan, and the other five municipalities each assigned one seat.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Valley_Regional_High_School_District#cite_note-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Valley_Regional_High_School_District#cite_note-32)

The **Northern Valley Regional High School District** is a comprehensive regional publichighschool district composed of two publichigh schools serving students in ninth through twelfth grades from Closter, Demarest, Harrington Park, Haworth, Northvale, Norwood and Old Tappan, suburban communities in Bergen County, in the U.S. state of New Jersey.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Valley_Regional_High_School_District#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Valley_Regional_High_School_District#cite_note-4) Students from Rockleigh attend the district as part of a sending/receiving relationship.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Valley_Regional_High_School_District#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Valley_Regional_High_School_District#cite_note-6)
As of the 2023–24 school year, the district, comprised of three schools, had an enrollment of 2,159 students and 236.1 classroom teachers (on an FTE basis), for a student–teacher ratio of 9.1:1.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Valley_Regional_High_School_District#cite_note-NCES-1)
The communities in the district, made up of upper-middle income families, consistently support the school budget, which provides for varied, in-depth college preparatory and career-oriented curricula. Courses range from the remedial to Advanced Placement.
The district participates in special education programs offered by Region III, one of seven such regional programs in Bergen County. Region III coordinates and develops special education programs for the 1,000 students with learning disabilities in the region, which includes the Northern Valley District, as well as those for the Alpine, Closter, Demarest, Harrington Park, Haworth, Northvale, Norwood and Old Tappan districts.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Valley_Regional_High_School_District#cite_note-7)
texts.3:
The district's first high school facility opened in Demarest in September 1955, before which students from the constituent municipalities attended Closter High School, Dumont High School or Tenafly High School.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Valley_Regional_High_School_District#cite_note-8)
After voters rejected a June 1959 referendum that would have raised $3.25 million for construction of the district's second high school in Old Tappan, voters narrowly approved a trimmed-down version of the plan in January 1960 that reduced the cost to $2.9 million (equivalent to $31.6 million in 2025). [[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Valley_Regional_High_School_District#cite_note-9)
The Old Tappan school was opened with 740 students between the 9th and 11th grades in March 1962 to address overcrowding in the district's original school at Demarest that had been holding split sessions before the new school opened.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Valley_Regional_High_School_District#cite_note-10) At its establishment, Northern Valley Old Tappan served students from Harrington Park, Northvale, Norwood and Old Tappan, as well as those from the northern portion of Closter.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Valley_Regional_High_School_District#cite_note-11)
The district had been classified by the New Jersey Department of Education as being in District Factor Group "I", the second-highest of eight groupings. District Factor Groups organize districts statewide to allow comparison by common socioeconomic characteristics of the local districts. From lowest socioeconomic status to highest, the categories are A, B, CD, DE, FG, GH, I and J.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Valley_Regional_High_School_District#cite_note-12)

The district's board of education, comprised of nine members, sets policy and oversees the fiscal and educational operation of the district through its administration. As a Type II school district, the board's trustees are elected directly by voters to serve three-year terms of office on a staggered basis, with three seats up for election each year held (since 2012) as part of the November general election. The board appoints a superintendent to oversee the district's day-to-day operations and a business administrator to supervise the business functions of the district.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Valley_Regional_High_School_District#cite_note-30) Seats on the board of education are allocated based on the population of the constituent municipalities, with two seats each allocated to Closter and Old Tappan, and the other five municipalities each assigned one seat.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Valley_Regional_High_School_District#cite_note-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Valley_Regional_High_School_District#cite_note-32)

The **Northern Valley Regional High School District** is a comprehensive regional publichighschool district composed of two publichigh schools serving students in ninth through twelfth grades from Closter, Demarest, Harrington Park, Haworth, Northvale, Norwood and Old Tappan, suburban communities in Bergen County, in the U.S. state of New Jersey.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Valley_Regional_High_School_District#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Valley_Regional_High_School_District#cite_note-4) Students from Rockleigh attend the district as part of a sending/receiving relationship.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Valley_Regional_High_School_District#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Valley_Regional_High_School_District#cite_note-6)
As of the 2023–24 school year, the district, comprised of three schools, had an enrollment of 2,159 students and 236.1 classroom teachers (on an FTE basis), for a student–teacher ratio of 9.1:1.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Valley_Regional_High_School_District#cite_note-NCES-1)
The communities in the district, made up of upper-middle income families, consistently support the school budget, which provides for varied, in-depth college preparatory and career-oriented curricula. Courses range from the remedial to Advanced Placement.
The district participates in special education programs offered by Region III, one of seven such regional programs in Bergen County. Region III coordinates and develops special education programs for the 1,000 students with learning disabilities in the region, which includes the Northern Valley District, as well as those for the Alpine, Closter, Demarest, Harrington Park, Haworth, Northvale, Norwood and Old Tappan districts.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Valley_Regional_High_School_District#cite_note-7)

The district's first high school facility opened in Demarest in September 1955, before which students from the constituent municipalities attended Closter High School, Dumont High School or Tenafly High School.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Valley_Regional_High_School_District#cite_note-8)
After voters rejected a June 1959 referendum that would have raised $3.25 million for construction of the district's second high school in Old Tappan, voters narrowly approved a trimmed-down version of the plan in January 1960 that reduced the cost to $2.9 million (equivalent to $31.6 million in 2025). [[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Valley_Regional_High_School_District#cite_note-9)
The Old Tappan school was opened with 740 students between the 9th and 11th grades in March 1962 to address overcrowding in the district's original school at Demarest that had been holding split sessions before the new school opened.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Valley_Regional_High_School_District#cite_note-10) At its establishment, Northern Valley Old Tappan served students from Harrington Park, Northvale, Norwood and Old Tappan, as well as those from the northern portion of Closter.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Valley_Regional_High_School_District#cite_note-11)
The district had been classified by the New Jersey Department of Education as being in District Factor Group "I", the second-highest of eight groupings. District Factor Groups organize districts statewide to allow comparison by common socioeconomic characteristics of the local districts. From lowest socioeconomic status to highest, the categories are A, B, CD, DE, FG, GH, I and J.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Valley_Regional_High_School_District#cite_note-12)

The district's board of education, comprised of nine members, sets policy and oversees the fiscal and educational operation of the district through its administration. As a Type II school district, the board's trustees are elected directly by voters to serve three-year terms of office on a staggered basis, with three seats up for election each year held (since 2012) as part of the November general election. The board appoints a superintendent to oversee the district's day-to-day operations and a business administrator to supervise the business functions of the district.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Valley_Regional_High_School_District#cite_note-30) Seats on the board of education are allocated based on the population of the constituent municipalities, with two seats each allocated to Closter and Old Tappan, and the other five municipalities each assigned one seat.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Valley_Regional_High_School_District#cite_note-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Valley_Regional_High_School_District#cite_note-32)

**Outagamie County** ( _OW-tə-GAY-mee_)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-1) is a county in the Fox Cities region of the U.S. state of Wisconsin, in the northeast of the state. As of the 2020 census, the population was 190,705.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-2020-census-55087-2) Its county seat is Appleton.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-GR6-3)

Outagamie County is part of the Appleton Metropolitan Statistical Area, which is itself part of the Appleton-Neenah-OshkoshCombined Statistical Area. It was named for the historic Meskwaki (Fox) people.
"Outagamie", a French transliteration of the Anishinaabe term for the Meskwaki (Fox) people, means "dwellers of the other shore" or "dwellers on the other side of the stream",[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-4) referring to their historic habitation along the St. Lawrence River and south of the Great Lakes. They occupied considerable territory in Wisconsin before colonization.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-5) Outagamie County was created in 1851 and organized in 1852.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-6) Before that, it was under the jurisdiction of Brown County.
According to the U.S. Census Bureau, the county has an area of 645 square miles (1,670 km 2), of which 638 square miles (1,650 km 2) is land and 7.1 square miles (18 km 2) (1.1%) is water.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-GR1-7)

Outagamie County is in northeast Wisconsin, covering 640 square miles along the Fox River, near the northern end of Lake Winnebago. It is the sixth-largest county by population in the state, behind Milwaukee, Dane, Waukesha, Brown, and Racine counties.
Map of the state of Wisconsin showing Outagamie County in red. Source: Wikimedia Commons, accessed March 2023.
Outagamie County is home to the Fox Cities, where most of the county’s population resides. The Fox Cities is the third-largest metropolitan area in the state, according to the county’s website. The county seat is Appleton. The county shares borders with Brown, Calumet, Shawano, Waupaca, and Winnebago counties.
We’ve collected a wealth of information about Outagamie County so taxpayers and residents can understand how county government operates and hold elected officials accountable. Click on the links below to learn about the county’s history and census details, how to contact elected officials, when public meetings take place, and much more. For the latest news,click here.
1.   **History**Everyone knows the hamburger was invented in 1885 in the Town of Seymour, located in Outagamie County. But we are also the home of the first hydroelectric central station in the United States and the first home in the world lighted by a hydroelectric station.  
2.   **Facts and Figures**Learn about the county’s geography, population, and economy — did you know the county’s median income is higher than the national average?  
3.   **Leadership**Contact information — including phone numbers, email, and mailing addresses for the county executive and 36 county supervisors.****  
4.   **Budget**The county’s 2023 budget is $420.3 million, a 30% increase over the 2022 budget. Learn more about where the money’s coming from … and going.  
5.   **Board Meeting Schedule, Agenda, Minutes**The County Board of Supervisors typically meets on the 2nd and 4th Tuesday of each month at 7:00 p.m. Click here to find meeting schedules, agendas, and minutes.
Joseph Bast

Joseph Bast was born and raised in the Fox Valley, graduated from Kimberly High School, and went to college and had a career in Chicago. After retiring in 2018, he returned to the Fox Valley and currently resides in Appleton’s new Riverheath community. He and his wife, Diane, created the Wisconsin Patriots Toolbox website and are active with Northeast Wisconsin Patriots and Appleton Concerned Taxpayers.

The tax roll marks parcels that are government-owned or enrolled in Wisconsin’s forest tax programs. In Outagamie County:
*   Federal-owned: 11,667 acres in 690 parcels  
*   State-owned: 11,467 acres in 430 parcels

In WI 2026, color the map by **Auxiliary Class of Property** to see these parcels, and tap one for the owner and acreage. The acreages are whole-parcel areas from the tax roll: a parcel that is only partly enrolled counts in full, and the tax roll doesn’t show posted areas or access routes. **Outagamie County** ( _OW-tə-GAY-mee_)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-1) is a county in the Fox Cities region of the U.S. state of Wisconsin, in the northeast of the state. As of the 2020 census, the population was 190,705.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-2020-census-55087-2) Its county seat is Appleton.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-GR6-3)
texts.1:
Outagamie County is part of the Appleton Metropolitan Statistical Area, which is itself part of the Appleton-Neenah-OshkoshCombined Statistical Area. It was named for the historic Meskwaki (Fox) people.
"Outagamie", a French transliteration of the Anishinaabe term for the Meskwaki (Fox) people, means "dwellers of the other shore" or "dwellers on the other side of the stream",[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-4) referring to their historic habitation along the St. Lawrence River and south of the Great Lakes. They occupied considerable territory in Wisconsin before colonization.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-5) Outagamie County was created in 1851 and organized in 1852.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-6) Before that, it was under the jurisdiction of Brown County.
According to the U.S. Census Bureau, the county has an area of 645 square miles (1,670 km 2), of which 638 square miles (1,650 km 2) is land and 7.1 square miles (18 km 2) (1.1%) is water.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-GR1-7)

Outagamie County's government consists of an elected County Board of Supervisors, a County Executive, and 36 county agencies and departments.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-outagamie.org-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-9)
The county executive serves as its chief executive officer, participating in the legislative process with the County Board of Supervisors and exercising administrative authority and control over the county's operations, departments, offices, boards, programs, and communications.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-10)
Department heads are appointed by the county executive, subject to the approval of the board of supervisors. The county executive also appoints members to the county's boards and commissions. The county executive sets the annual budget in consultation with and subject to the approval of the board of supervisors.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-11)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-outagamie.org-8)
County Executive Tom Nelson was first elected in 2011.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outagamie_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-12)

## Outagamie County Topographic Map
The land here in Outagamie County is relatively flat, with long stretches of fertile plains. However, the Fox River flows through the county, carving a shallow valley through Appleton. While there aren’t steep hills, subtle changes in elevation are noticeable near waterways.

## Outagamie County Road Map
Interstate 41 cuts diagonally through Outagamie County in the southeast corner. Even though that’s the main route, local roads branch off into farm fields and smaller towns. Traffic picks up near Appleton, but it’s manageable.

## Outagamie County Satellite Map
Appleton pops out near Fox River, with gray city blocks packed along its banks. The rest of the county alternates between green farmland and small forested patches. Other notable rivers are Wolf, Rat, and Embarrass Rivers.

**Brown County** is a county in the U.S. state of Wisconsin. As of the 2020 census, the population was 268,740,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-QF-1) making it the fourth-most populous county in Wisconsin. The county seat is Green Bay.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-GR6-2) Brown County is part of the Green Bay metropolitan area.

[](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tourist's_Pocket_Map_Of_Michigan_(Samuel_Augustus_Mitchell,_1835).jpg)
Wisconsin Territory depicted on this 1835 _Tourist's Pocket Map Of Michigan_, showing a Menominee-filled Brown County, Wisconsin that spans the northern half of the territory.
Brown County is one of Wisconsin's two original counties, along with Crawford County. It originally spanned the entire eastern half of the state when formed by the Michigan Territorial legislature in 1818._[citation needed_] It was named for Major General Jacob Brown, a military leader during the War of 1812.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-4)
Several towns along the Fox River vied for the position of county seat in Brown County's early years. The first county seat was located at Menomoneeville (now a part of Allouez) in 1824. In 1837, a public referendum relocated the county seat to De Pere. The location was put up for the popular vote again in 1854, resulting in the establishment of the present county seat at Green Bay.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-HNW-5)
The oldest known tree in Wisconsin, a 1,300-year-old cedar growing on the Niagara Escarpment, was found in Brown County.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-6)
According to the U.S. Census Bureau, the county has a total area of 616 square miles (1,600 km 2), of which 530 square miles (1,400 km 2) is land and 86 square miles (220 km 2) (14%) is water.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-GR1-7)

**Brown County** is a county in the U.S. state of Wisconsin. As of the 2020 census, the population was 268,740,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-QF-1) making it the fourth-most populous county in Wisconsin. Wisconsin Territory depicted on this 1835 _Tourist's Pocket Map Of Michigan_, showing a Menominee-filled Brown County, Wisconsin that spans the northern half of the territory.
Brown County is one of Wisconsin's two original counties, along with Crawford County. It originally spanned the entire eastern half of the state when formed by the Michigan Territorial legislature in 1818._[citation needed_] It was named for Major General Jacob Brown, a military leader during the War of 1812.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-4)
Several towns along the Fox River vied for the position of county seat in Brown County's early years. The first county seat was located at Menomoneeville (now a part of Allouez) in 1824. In 1837, a public referendum relocated the county seat to De Pere. The location was put up for the popular vote again in 1854, resulting in the establishment of the present county seat at Green Bay.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-HNW-5)
The oldest known tree in Wisconsin, a 1,300-year-old cedar growing on the Niagara Escarpment, was found in Brown County.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-6)
According to the U.S. Census Bureau, the county has a total area of 616 square miles (1,600 km 2), of which 530 square miles (1,400 km 2) is land and 86 square miles (220 km 2) (14%) is water.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-GR1-7)

### Political representation
[edit]
The current Wisconsin Legislative districts were defined in the law 2023 Wisconsin Act 94, passed by the legislature and signed by the Governor in February 2024. The current congressional districts were defined by the Wisconsin Supreme Court decision _Johnson v. Wisconsin Elections Commission_ in April 2022.
For representation in the U.S. House of Representatives, Brown County falls entirely within [Wisconsin's 8th congressional district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin's_8th_congressional_district "Wisconsin's 8th congressional district"), currently represented by Republican Tony Wied, since November 2024.
In the Wisconsin Senate, Brown County fully contains one Senate district (the 30th), and makes up a portion of two other districts (the 1st and 2nd).
*   the [1st Senate district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin's_1st_Senate_district "Wisconsin's 1st Senate district") contains the rural eastern and southern parts of Brown County along with the neighboring Door Peninsula, and is represented by Republican André Jacque of De Pere.  
*   the [2nd Senate district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin's_2nd_Senate_district "Wisconsin's 2nd Senate district") contains the rural northwestern quadrant of Brown County and vast areas of surrounding counties, and is represented by Republican Eric Wimberger of Oconto.  
*   the [30th Senate district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin's_30th_Senate_district "Wisconsin's 30th Senate district") contains the core urban and suburban areas of Green Bay, De Pere, Ashwaubenon, and Allouez, and is represented by Democrat Jamie Wall of Green Bay.
In the Wisconsin State Assembly, Brown County fully contains three Assembly districts (88th, 89th, and 90th), and makes up a portion of five other districts (the 1st, 2nd, 4th, 5th, and 6th).

**Brown County** is a county in the U.S. state of Wisconsin. As of the 2020 census, the population was 268,740,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-QF-1) making it the fourth-most populous county in Wisconsin. The county seat is Green Bay.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-GR6-2) Brown County is part of the Green Bay metropolitan area.

[](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tourist's_Pocket_Map_Of_Michigan_(Samuel_Augustus_Mitchell,_1835).jpg)
Wisconsin Territory depicted on this 1835 _Tourist's Pocket Map Of Michigan_, showing a Menominee-filled Brown County, Wisconsin that spans the northern half of the territory.
Brown County is one of Wisconsin's two original counties, along with Crawford County. It originally spanned the entire eastern half of the state when formed by the Michigan Territorial legislature in 1818._[citation needed_] It was named for Major General Jacob Brown, a military leader during the War of 1812.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-4)
Several towns along the Fox River vied for the position of county seat in Brown County's early years. The first county seat was located at Menomoneeville (now a part of Allouez) in 1824. In 1837, a public referendum relocated the county seat to De Pere. The location was put up for the popular vote again in 1854, resulting in the establishment of the present county seat at Green Bay.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-HNW-5)
The oldest known tree in Wisconsin, a 1,300-year-old cedar growing on the Niagara Escarpment, was found in Brown County.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-6)
According to the U.S. Census Bureau, the county has a total area of 616 square miles (1,600 km 2), of which 530 square miles (1,400 km 2) is land and 86 square miles (220 km 2) (14%) is water.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown_County,_Wisconsin#cite_note-GR1-7)

### Political representation
[edit]
The current Wisconsin Legislative districts were defined in the law 2023 Wisconsin Act 94, passed by the legislature and signed by the Governor in February 2024. The current congressional districts were defined by the Wisconsin Supreme Court decision _Johnson v. Wisconsin Elections Commission_ in April 2022.
For representation in the U.S. House of Representatives, Brown County falls entirely within [Wisconsin's 8th congressional district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin's_8th_congressional_district "Wisconsin's 8th congressional district"), currently represented by Republican Tony Wied, since November 2024.
In the Wisconsin Senate, Brown County fully contains one Senate district (the 30th), and makes up a portion of two other districts (the 1st and 2nd).
*   the [1st Senate district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin's_1st_Senate_district "Wisconsin's 1st Senate district") contains the rural eastern and southern parts of Brown County along with the neighboring Door Peninsula, and is represented by Republican André Jacque of De Pere.  
*   the [2nd Senate district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin's_2nd_Senate_district "Wisconsin's 2nd Senate district") contains the rural northwestern quadrant of Brown County and vast areas of surrounding counties, and is represented by Republican Eric Wimberger of Oconto.  
*   the [30th Senate district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin's_30th_Senate_district "Wisconsin's 30th Senate district") contains the core urban and suburban areas of Green Bay, De Pere, Ashwaubenon, and Allouez, and is represented by Democrat Jamie Wall of Green Bay.
In the Wisconsin State Assembly, Brown County fully contains three Assembly districts (88th, 89th, and 90th), and makes up a portion of five other districts (the 1st, 2nd, 4th, 5th, and 6th).
